newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian long-term interest rates unlikely to fall.
newsitem.headline: Indian long-term interest rates unlikely to fall.

text.p: India's short-term interest rates have fallen in the past six months due to slower industrial demand but long-term rates are seen remaining at current high levels, bankers and analysts said on Friday.
"Demand for long-term funds exceeds supply," former Reserve Bank of India (RBI) governor S. Venkitaramanan told Reuters. "This will keep interest rates high."

Short-term rates have come down sharply due to poor demand from industry, analysts said. Bank credit fell by 16.44 billion rupees ($460 million) to 2,688.63 billion between March 29 and August 30, 1996, according to latest RBI figures.
Further, RBI cuts in cash reserve requirements in April and July this year freed 93 billion rupees to banks.
Primary market yields on 91-day treasury bills have fallen to around 10 percent from 13 percent in March while commercial paper is now priced around 13 percent against 17 to 18 percent.
Prime lending rates have also eased with some banks slashing rates by up to 100 basis points in less than three months.
State-run banks, who dominate the banking industry with more than 80 percent of total bank advances, announced a 50 basis point cut in prime rates in July.

Industry leader State Bank of India (SBI) announced a second 50 basis point cut to 15.5 percent per annum earlier this month. Two other state-run banks have announced similar cuts and others are expected to follow suit.
Analysts said long-term interest rates, however, show no signs of easing with term-lending financial firms borrowing at an effective cost of over 17 percent for maturities above 20 years.
Leading companies like Larsen & Toubro and Tata Iron and Steel Company recently raised funds for 10 years and more at rates in excess of 17 percent.
"Even the government is unable to significantly cut rates on its long term stock (government securities)," an analyst said.
"Last June, it issued 10-year stock at 13.85 percent against 14 percent in 1995.
"But last week's six-year stock issue flopped with just over 50 percent subscription despite 13.82 percent yield," he added.
"Government borrowings convey a strong signal to the rest of the financial market," a senior official at India's leading term lender, Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI) said.
"At the moment the signals are that interest rates will remain at the current level."

The current paradox of banks facing declining credit disbursals and being forced to cut interest, while term lenders and corporates borrow at high rates may be due to structural rigidities within the financial system, Venkitaramanan said.

"We also have to realise that this may be a temporary phenomenon," he said. "As industrial activity picks up in the busy season (October to April), demand for credit will rise and even short-term rates will go up."
The solution lies in attracting foreign capital inflows into the country, analysts said.

"Basically, our requirements cannot be met though domestic sources," said Aashish Pitale, analyst at ICICI Securities and Finance Company. The recent government decision to allow foreign insitutional investors to set up funds to invest exclusively in Indian corporate was an important step in this regard, he said.
